transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-20
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Leo Chen (Redwood SE), Jordan Reyes (CTO, Atlas), Priya Singh (Head of Platform, Atlas), Evan Moore (SRE, Atlas)

Summary (auto):
Quick technical deep dive on autoscaling strategies for Redwood Dedicated / Private deployments. Discussed burst policies, queueing/latency tradeoffs, reserved GPUs vs. burst pools, KV cache warmup, batching and quantization impacts on throughput and latency. Agreed to run a 24h benchmark and share capacity planner spreadsheet.

Topics: autoscaling policy options, burst capacity, queue-length based scaling, reserved GPU sizing, cold-starts and KV cache, batching configs, quantization tradeoffs, VPC/on-prem constraints (KMS, private registry).

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): okay everyone welcome thanks for making time today, this is Maya from Redwood, I'll hand to Leo for the deep dive in a sec but quick roll call.
[00:06] Jordan (Atlas): yep Jordan here, Priya and Evan on our side also.
[00:10] Priya (Atlas): hi hi, Priya.
[00:12] Evan (Atlas): Evan, morning.
[00:14] Leo (Redwood SE): hey all, Leo here, thanks Jordan. We're gonna focus on autoscale and capacity planning, sort of practical knobs you can turn for predictable p95 and cost.

[00:30] Leo (Redwood SE): first, quick context: Redwood supports hosted, dedicated and private. For Dedicated/Private you can reserve GPU pools, set burst policies to allow extra capacity, or rely on autoscaler rules. There's a tradeoff: reserved gives predictability and cost-savings at scale, burst gives headroom but more variable e2e latency and cost.

[01:05] Jordan (Atlas): our use case: customer-facing assistants -- roughly 300 rps peak per region, lots of short chat turns but occasional long context (up to 2k tokens). We need ~p95 under 350ms for prompt-only responses, and 95th for full chat ideally under 700ms. Also strict data residency and SOC2.

[01:36] Leo (Redwood SE): got it. Two immediate patterns we recommend: steady-state reserved pools sized for baseline throughput, plus a small burst pool for spikes. Use queue-length metrics for reactive scaling and a warm pool to reduce cold-starts.

[02:05] Priya (Atlas): queue-length metrics: do you mean request queue depth into the serving runtime? Is that an internal metric? We need to plug to our Datadog.

[02:20] Leo (Redwood SE): yes, queue length we expose as a metric; scaling rules can be based on tokens-in-queue or request-depth. For Dedicated/Private we can emit to your metrics (Datadog, Prometheus). The basic model: scale up when queue > X for Y seconds, scale down with cooldown to avoid flapping.

[02:50] Maya (Redwood AE): folks usually tune X to maintain p95 SLO, e.g. X=50 requests or tokens-per-second threshold; we'll help calibrate with the capacity planner.

[03:12] Evan (Atlas): we worry about tail latency from batching; sometimes batching helps throughput but spikes tail latencies. How do you balance batching versus single-request latency?

[03:28] Leo (Redwood SE): great question. Redwood runtime supports dynamic batching with max latency budgets and batch size caps. You can set a per-route latency budget: if a request is waiting > budget it gets flushed immediately. So you get throughput from batching but bounded tail. There's also adaptive batching where the runtime adjusts batch sizes based on observed latency.

[03:58] Priya (Atlas): does adaptive batching work well with KV cache warm-up? Our workload has many repeated prefixes so cache hit rate is high after warm-up, but cold starts kill latency.

[04:14] Leo (Redwood SE): yes, KV cache significantly reduces per-token compute for long-context generation. Important considerations: when you scale horizontally (add replicas), each new replica has empty KV; warm pool of pre-initialized replicas helps. Also persistent KV snapshots (for Private deployment) can reduce warm start. We recommend keeping a warm pool of at least 1-2 replicas per zone.

[04:42] Jordan (Atlas): warm pool costs money though. How do we compute tradeoff?

[04:48] Leo (Redwood SE): capacity planner spreadsheet factors reserved GPU cost, warm pool size, expected spike frequency and spike width. If spikes are common and short, warm pool + burst capacity is cheaper and better for tail latency than cold-scaling. We'll run numbers with your traffic profile.

[05:10] Maya (Redwood AE): (link) capacity spreadsheet: https://redwood.example.com/planner/atlas-capacity.xlsx we'll populate with your sample traffic.

[05:22] Evan (Atlas): noted. On quantization: we have some models run in int8 for cost reasons. How does quantization affect throughput and KV compatibility?

[05:32] Leo (Redwood SE): quantization reduces memory and increases inference throughput on many GPUs, but careful: 8-bit kernels sometimes change generation speed and can affect output quality. KV cache compatibility: the runtime supports quantized KV paths; however, some models see different cache hit perf depending on kernel support. We'll recommend model-specific quant profiles: Redwood Optimize can suggest these from your evals.

[06:05] Priya (Atlas): any impact on tail latencies?

[06:09] Leo (Redwood SE): typically quantized paths reduce per-token time, so tail improves; the caveat is if quantization increases variability because of fallback kernels on certain hardware, then you get jitter. We'll test on your hardware or our equivalent.

[06:34] Jordan (Atlas): about burst policies: what units are we reserving? GPUs? or concurrency units?

[06:44] Maya (Redwood AE): you reserve GPU pools (N GPUs of X type) for Dedicated; burst policies allow temporary allocation from a shared pool or allow autoscaler to spin additional instances (on the same cluster or cloud region). We also support soft-reserved capacity where you buy committed capacity with burst credits.

[07:05] Evan (Atlas): in our cloud procurement we'd prefer committed reservations with predictable monthly cost. How does Redwood price reserved vs burst?

[07:14] Maya (Redwood AE): reserved is priced as monthly commit per-GPU. Burst is billed on usage; we can model the blended cost in the planner. For procurement, committed pools simplify budgeting and meet your finance needs.

[07:30] Leo (Redwood SE): for scaling triggers: we recommend multi-signal autoscaling: primary signal queue length (tokens-in-queue), secondary GPU util, and observed tail latency. Queue length is responsive; GPU util avoids over-scaling for bad requests. Use cooldown windows and a fast-path for immediate small bursts.

[07:55] Priya (Atlas): can we set a per-route SLO and have the autoscaler behave differently per route? e.g., high-priority route has larger warm pool.

[08:05] Leo (Redwood SE): yep, routing policies per-route and per-model. You can pin routes to specific pools, set different warm pool sizes, and set priority-based queueing. That way critical routes get reserved capacity and lower-priority ones run on shared/burst.

[08:28] Jordan (Atlas): about queueing models: what's the recommended queueing discipline? FIFO, priority, fair-share?

[08:35] Leo (Redwood SE): Redwood supports FIFO and priority queues; we often recommend priority with weight-based fairness if you have mixed workloads. For your case, customer chat should be priority over background batch ranking. Also set max-queue depth per priority to avoid head-of-line blocking.

[09:02] Evan (Atlas): and observability: what metrics do you expose so we can correlate SLOs with scale events?

[09:10] Leo (Redwood SE): we emit request-rate, tokens-per-second, queue-depth, per-route latency percentiles (p50/p95/p99), GPU utilization, memory pressure, KV hit-rate, batch-size distribution, and scale events (scale up/down + reasons). All ingestable into Datadog or your SIEM.

[09:36] Priya (Atlas): security question: on private deployment we need KMS/HSM integration and audit logs. How does that change autoscaling?

[09:45] Maya (Redwood AE): functionally autoscaling is the same; operationally you need network egress to image registries if using dynamic burst instances, or you pre-cache container images in your private registry. KMS calls are usually to your cloud KMS or HSM endpoint; we support that. For on-prem air-gapped, you'd typically pre-provision warm pools and avoid dynamic provisioning.

[10:12] Jordan (Atlas): OK makes sense. What about cold-start times: how long to spin up a warm replica that includes model weights and warmed KV?

[10:22] Leo (Redwood SE): depends on model size and hardware. For a 20B model on a typical GPU, cold-start (pull model + load weights + JIT/kernels) could be ~90-180s. Warm pool eviction/rehydration is the issue. With warm snapshot or persistent memory and warm images, we can get warm start to ~20-30s in best case. That's why warm pools are important for low tail latency.

[10:54] Evan (Atlas): do you recommend using smaller sharded models so startup is faster?

[11:00] Leo (Redwood SE): sharded models add complexity; sharding across GPUs reduces per-GPU memory but increases interconnect overhead. If your workload needs lower cold-starts, smaller or quantized variants are an option; we can also use model variants for cost/latency tiers and automatic fallback on high load.

[11:25] Priya (Atlas): about automatic fallback: if primary model is saturated do you reroute to a smaller model automatically?

[11:33] Leo (Redwood SE): yes, routing policies can define fallback chains: e.g., model-x -> quantized-model-x -> distilled-model-x. You can set degradation policies and acceptable quality thresholds. We also support A/B to measure user-visible regression.

[11:50] Jordan (Atlas): any guidance on sizing reserved GPUs for our 300 rps peak with mixed short+long contexts?

[11:58] Leo (Redwood SE): preliminary calc: we need to estimate avg tokens-per-request and average generation length. With your sample 300 rps peak and say 30 tokens per response average, that's 9k tokens/s. On A100-class hardware a 20B model with quantization might do ~1.5-2k tokens/s per GPU (rough estimate), so we'd need ~5 GPUs for the peak baseline plus additional for overhead and headroom — so baseline 6 reserved GPUs and 2-3 for burst/warm pool is a starting point. We'll refine after benchmarking.

[12:36] Maya (Redwood AE): note those are rough, we'll run the capacity planner with your real payload distribution.

[12:45] Evan (Atlas): what about cost for that reserved configuration?

[12:48] Maya (Redwood AE): we'll show committed cost vs blended with burst in the spreadsheet. Committed tends to be cheaper per-GPU but you pay for unused capacity, so burst credits can lower expected monthly spend if spikes are rare.

[13:05] Priya (Atlas): on the benchmarking you mentioned, what does Redwood need from us?

[13:11] Leo (Redwood SE): we need a traffic snapshot: request timing, token lengths, route labels (priority), and 7-day tail latency logs if possible. Also confirm model variants you want tested and deployment target (Dedicated in Redwood cloud vs Private in your VPC). We'll run 24h synthetic runs against a dedicated pool to measure p50/p95/p99 and cost.

[13:38] Jordan (Atlas): we can provide the traffic dump and an anonymized sample. Evan will pull the logs.

[13:45] Evan (Atlas): yep I'll upload to the shared folder.

[13:48] Maya (Redwood AE): great. A few operational notes: 1) use cooldown windows to avoid flapping, 2) don't scale down below warm-pool floor, 3) use priority queues to avoid head-of-line blocking.

[14:05] Leo (Redwood SE): small detail on batching: if you expect many short requests, set max-latency-budget low (e.g., 10-20ms) so batches don't wait too long; for background throughput routes you can allow up to 50-100ms. Also we emit batch-size histograms so you can tune.

[14:30] Priya (Atlas): what happens to KV cache when instance is preempted or evicted?

[14:36] Leo (Redwood SE): if evicted, KV is lost unless using persistent snapshots; results in cold cache. For critical routes we recommend replication of warm KV snapshots or sticky routing to warm replicas.

[14:52] Jordan (Atlas): do you have any recommended queue-length thresholds as a starting point?

[14:58] Leo (Redwood SE): common starting rule: scale up when queue > 50 requests for > 30s, scale down when queue == 0 for > 5 minutes (with floor warm pool). But these numbers depend heavily on token size and generation cost. We'll tune with the benchmark.

[15:18] Evan (Atlas): if we do Private on-prem with no dynamic provisioning, is autoscaling still workable?

[15:26] Leo (Redwood SE): autoscaling becomes capacity-aware scaling: you're limited to adding pre-provisioned warm replicas or spinning containers on existing nodes. For strictly air-gapped on-prem you typically provision a larger baseline and rely on load-leveling and priority queues. Warm pools and pre-cached images become critical.

[15:48] Priya (Atlas): for VPC option in our cloud, can Redwood provision autoscaling that uses our account to spin instances?

[15:56] Maya (Redwood AE): yes, Redwood Private supports a customer-managed control plane where we use your IAM role to provision instances in your account; images and KMS calls stay in your VPC. We'll share the architecture docs in follow-up.

[16:12] Jordan (Atlas): any gotchas around network egress for models or container pulls?

[16:17] Leo (Redwood SE): if you restrict egress, pre-cache container images and model weights in your private registry or a pre-signed S3 bucket. For dynamic burst you need temporary egress to pull images — unless you rely on a shared image cache.

[16:35] Maya (Redwood AE): we'll include a checklist for VPC/on-prem provisioning with the docs.

[16:42] Priya (Atlas): about model variants and fallback: how do you measure quality degradation?

[16:48] Leo (Redwood SE): we tie quality regressions to eval suites and live prompt tests. For POC we can run A/B with a small percent of traffic and measure conversion or automated eval metrics. Redwood Optimize recommends candidates based on eval pass/fail.

[17:05] Jordan (Atlas): timeline: we'd like a POC to start next week if possible.

[17:10] Maya (Redwood AE): we can kickoff POC on 2026-04-28 — I'll send calendar invite after this call once we confirm the traffic file and licensing.

[17:19] Evan (Atlas): works for us.

[17:22] Priya (Atlas): one more quick question: what's the behavior when a GPU goes OOM during a spike?

[17:28] Leo (Redwood SE): runtime isolates OOM at request granularity when possible and fails fast to avoid cascading. We also have circuit-breakers per-route to stop large requests from taking down a node. OOM events emit to logs and trigger scale-up if it's resource-pressure related.

[17:48] Jordan (Atlas): cool. Anything else?

[17:51] Maya (Redwood AE): quick recap of next steps: Maya share planner and pricing; Leo run benchmarks once Atlas uploads traffic; Atlas to upload logs and confirm model variants; schedule POC kickoff 2026-04-28.

[18:08] Priya (Atlas): thanks all, valuable discussion.

[18:11] Evan (Atlas): thanks.

[18:13] Leo (Redwood SE): thanks, talk soon.

End of transcript.

Notes: There are a few transcription artifacts (names and acronyms sometimes off). References: capacity planner (link above), Redwood Private architecture doc (to be shared), benchmark scripts (redwood-bench v1.3 link will be provided).
